title: National Park Service — Allegheny Portage Railroad
claims: Portage opened March 18, 1834, linking Hollidaysburg and Johnstown through ten inclined planes, five on each side of the mountains.
Stationary steam engines pulled cars by ropes on the inclines; locomotives worked more level stretches.
The combined canal-and-rail journey between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh took about four days.
Horseshoe Curve and the PRR continuous rail crossing opened February 15, 1854.
PRR purchased the state canal system in 1857 and took possession August 1.

title: National Park Service — Horseshoe Curve nomination, NRIS 66000647
claims: The nomination credits J. Edgar Thomson with concentrating the steep climb in approximately 9.8 miles west of Altoona, rather than maintaining a higher route far to the east.
The east-slope design called for a maximum grade of 1.8 percent after a resurvey in 1850.
Construction used a cut at Kittanning Point and fills across Kittanning Run and Glenwhite Run.
The nomination describes a 220-degree central angle, original double track, a third track completed in 1898 and a fourth in 1900.
Its cost estimate of $2,495,000 applies to the entire 31.1-mile Altoona–Johnstown segment excluding the summit tunnel, not to the curve alone.

title: Federal Railroad Administration — RR 22-29, October 2022
claims: The technical report describes approximately 2,375 feet of curve length, 1,300 feet diameter, a 1.8 percent grade and three main tracks.
FRA/AAR research measured rail forces and fastener demand at the curve in 2022.
The field study sampled 55 trains during one 24-hour window; this is not an average daily traffic claim.
Train makeup, traction, braking and temperature affected rail forces; the study addressed fatigue in track fasteners.

title: Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission — The Horseshoe Curve, 1858
claims: Irish immigrant laborers worked in camps, using hand tools and mule-drawn carts to cut the mountain and fill ravines.
PRR promoted the curve through passenger announcements, calendars and publicity.
A station served sightseers in 1865; the railroad beautified the site in 1879; a model appeared at the 1893 Columbian Exposition.
William T. Purviance made the documented albumen photograph circa 1858.

title: American Society of Civil Engineers — Horseshoe Curve, Pennsylvania Railroad
claims: Opening the mountain route strengthened Philadelphia’s access to western commerce against rival ports.
A Harrisburg newspaper report dated February 15, 1854 described the Philadelphia–Pittsburgh trip as fifteen hours.
The earthwork relied on manual labor, blasting powder and animal power.

title: City of Altoona — History of Altoona
claims: The Pennsylvania Railroad was chartered in 1846.
The railroad began developing Altoona in 1849 as a staging area for line construction.
The city’s location and growth were tied to the mountain approach.

title: Historic American Buildings Survey — City of Altoona, Library of Congress
claims: Altoona’s shops supported helper locomotives and system maintenance.
Railroad engineers laid out the town in 1849 around the tracks and shops.
Documented population: about 2,000 in 1854; 10,618 in 1870; 30,337 in 1890; 60,331 in 1920.

title: National Library of New Zealand — Associated Press report, Levin Daily Chronicle, July 3, 1942
claims: This contemporary Associated Press report explicitly identifies Horseshoe Curve as a planned target of the German submarine-landed sabotage teams.
The report also describes arrests of residents around Altoona; allegations and wartime arrests must not be represented as convictions or proof of guilt.

title: Federal Bureau of Investigation — Nazi Saboteurs and George Dasch
claims: Eight German saboteurs landed in two teams in New York and Florida in June 1942.
George Dasch’s disclosures helped investigators find the other men.
All eight had been arrested by June 27, 1942, without carrying out an act of destruction.
This FBI summary does not itself name Horseshoe Curve; pair with S08 for that claim.

title: Railroaders Memorial Museum — K4 1361 History
claims: K4s 1361 entered service from Altoona’s Juniata Shops on May 18, 1918 and retired in 1956.
It was displayed as a steam-era monument at Horseshoe Curve in 1957.
The locomotive left the curve in 1985 and made its first restored run April 12, 1987.

title: Railroaders Memorial Museum — Rolling Stock
claims: The PRR GP9 diesel-electric locomotive 7048, built in December 1955, replaced 1361 on display at the curve in 1985.
The museum preserves the former east-approach position-light signal bridge from Horseshoe Curve.

title: NPS NPGallery — National Register record 66000647
claims: The federal record dates the Horseshoe Curve historic designation to November 13, 1966.
Areas of significance are engineering and transportation.

title: Pennsylvania State Archives — Penn Central Railroad Collection, MG-286
claims: Pennsylvania Railroad merged with New York Central in 1968 to form Penn Central.
Penn Central entered bankruptcy in 1970.

title: Conrail — Company History
claims: Conrail began operations April 1, 1976 to revive rail service in the Northeast and Midwest.
Conrail became profitable in 1981 and returned to private ownership through a 1987 public stock offering.
The 1999 restructuring divided most assets between Norfolk Southern and CSX; Conrail continued as a shared switching and terminal railroad.

title: Norfolk Southern — On its 30th anniversary, June 1, 2012
claims: Norfolk Southern acquired a large part of Conrail on June 1, 1999.

title: Railroaders Memorial Museum — About
claims: The Railroaders Memorial Museum opened in 1980 through a local preservation effort.
The museum acquired operation of the Horseshoe Curve visitor center and observation park in the early 1990s after a public partnership renovated the site.
Rail work shaped Altoona’s neighborhoods, shifts and daily life; the end of steam brought employment changes.

title: Amtrak — Philadelphia station, Pennsylvanian route highlights
claims: Amtrak identifies Horseshoe Curve as a scenic highlight of the Pennsylvanian between New York and Pittsburgh.

title: Norfolk Southern — Best places to safely catch NS trains in Pennsylvania, June 16, 2026
claims: Norfolk Southern still identifies the curve as an active public train-viewing destination on its network in 2026.

title: Library of Congress — A. P. McDowell, The Horseshoe Curve, October 12, 1934
claims: Panoramic photograph showing the mature four-track landscape.
LOC rights advisory: no known restrictions on publication; no renewal found.

title: Library of Congress — Joseph Pennell, Horse shoe curve, P.R.R., 1919
claims: Etching by Joseph Pennell, published in 1919.
LOC rights advisory: no known restrictions on publication.

title: National Park Service — List of National Historic Landmarks by State
claims: The official National Historic Landmarks list identifies Horseshoe Curve in Blair County, Pennsylvania, with a designation date of November 13, 1966.
